China has five “autonomous regions”. Together they cover close to half of the country's land area and hold well under a tenth of its people.

What autonomy actually means in China — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The five are Xinjiang, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Ningxia and Guangxi. Each was built around a designated minority: Uyghurs, Tibetans, Mongols, Hui Muslims and Zhuang. Each sits on a frontier — which is the point. The status maps China's edges, not its centre.

2/ Guangxi is the odd one out: not remote, but coastal and on the Vietnamese border. Its Zhuang population, around 18 million, is China's largest single ethnic minority — a group most people outside China have never heard of.

3/ Inner Mongolia is home to more ethnic Mongols than Mongolia itself: roughly 4 million, against a total Mongolian population near 3.5 million. The independent nation-state is smaller than the Chinese region named after the same people.

4/ On paper these regions can adapt national law, use minority languages in schools and courts, and reserve the top government post for a member of the titular group. In practice the Party secretary outranks the governor — and is almost always Han.

5/ The second map shows where separatist movements exist. Three regions appear on both maps: Xinjiang, Tibet and Inner Mongolia. Autonomy on paper and independence movements in fact have turned out to be the same geography.

6/ In 2020, plans to cut Mongolian-language instruction in Inner Mongolia's schools put students and parents into the streets — rare open protest there. Language policy is where autonomy gets tested first, and usually loses.

The design is old and deliberate: name a region for its minority, grant symbolic powers, keep security and the Party chain of command central. Nearly half of China's territory is governed that way.
